body:
# From Greek to Unicode: the journey of Drákōn

Long before it was a domain, this name traveled through scripts. **Drákōn** begins in Greek, passes through scholarly transliteration, and ends — for now — inside the punycode machinery of the global DNS. Each stage of that journey preserves some information and loses some, and the craft of restoration is knowing exactly which marks matter. This post follows the name stage by stage: the original script, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the material evidence, and finally the Unicode form that carries all of it into the address bar. Think of it as a biography of a name, told through its spelling.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Drákōn
- **ASCII form:** drakon
- **Meaning:** "'The one who sees clearly' (from δέρκομαι, to see)"
- **Domain of influence:** Serpent, Guardian, Vigilance
- **Pantheon:** Greek
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** Δράκων (Greek)
- **Live domain:** drákōn.com

## Overview

**Drákōn** (*drakon*) — The Sleepless Watcher — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Serpent, Guardian, Vigilance". The name means "'The one who sees clearly' (from δέρκομαι, to see)".

Drákōn is not the fire-breathing hoard-guard of medieval romance but the Greeks' older idea: the enormous serpent that guards — a spring, a tree, a golden fleece, a goddess's shrine. His name comes from the verb "to see": the dragon is the one who never blinks.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Drákōn** and serves its temple at [drákōn.com](https://xn--drkn-6na36d.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *drakon* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Greek as **Δράκων**. Etymologically it means "'The one who sees clearly' (from δέρκομαι, to see)".

The ASCII form *drakon* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Drákōn** recovers both the stress accent and the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **d** → **D** — Same letter
- **r** → **r** — Same letter
- **a** → **á** — Stress mark (acute/tone)
- **k** → **k** — Same letter
- **o** → **ō** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **n** → **n** — Same letter

Attested and derived spellings of the name:

- **Drakōn** — macron-only form: LSJ convention: length only, no stress mark

The project holds the domain **drákōn.com** (xn--drkn-6na36d.com) as the canonical home of this name.

## The Original Script

The name is written in Greek as **Δράκων**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *drakon* and the PuniCodex restoration **Drákōn** are measured: the restoration preserves both its pitch accent and its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/drá.kɔːn/** — Attic Greek.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: DRAH-kone, stress on the first syllable with a long final ō.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — δράκων
- **Latin** — draco
- **English** — dragon
- **Owned form** — Drákōn

Greek δράκων derives from the aorist root of δέρκομαι, "to see clearly" — the dragon is etymologically "the sharp-sighted one," the watcher. The circumflex in Drákōn marks the long ō of the -ων stem; the macron-only Drakōn is the scholarly fallback. The ō of the oblique stem (drakontos) is the vowel the macron preserves — the nominative lengthens it from the root.

## Mythology

Every Greek dragon is a threshold made flesh: kill one and a sanctuary, a city, or a marriage becomes possible — which is why the founders of cities are all, sooner or later, dragonslayers.

### Apóllōn and Python (The Oracle)

The Homeric Hymn to Apóllōn tells how the god, seeking a site for his oracle, found the spring at Delphoi guarded by a great she-dragon who had nursed Typhaon and ravaged the flocks. He shot her and left her to rot in the sun — "now rot (pytheu) here upon the fruitful soil" — and the place was called Pythō, the priestess Pythia, ever after.

### Kadmos at the Spring (The City)

Sent to fetch water from the Ismenian spring, Kadmos' companions were killed by its guardian dragon, offspring of Árēs. Kadmos crushed it with a rock, and on Athēnā's counsel sowed half its teeth: armed men, the Spartoi, rose from the furrows and killed each other until five remained — the ancestors of Thebes' noble houses.

### Ladon of the Hesperides (The Apples)

Beyond Atlas, at the world's western edge, the dragon Ladon — offspring of Phorkys and Ketō, in Hesiod "terrible, with a hundred voices" — coiled around the tree of the golden apples that Gaia gave at Hēra's wedding. Hēraklēs' eleventh labour took the apples; the wounded or slain dragon was set among the stars as the constellation Draco, coiled around the north celestial pole.

### The Kolchian Warden (The Fleece)

The Golden Fleece hung in Árēs' grove at Kolchis, guarded by a dragon "vast as a fifty-oared ship" that Apollonius says never closed its eyes in sleep. Mēdeia's song and her pharmaka drenched it in slumber — the rare Greek dragon defeated not by force but by knowledge.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Drákōn concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The coil** — The guarding embrace; energy held in reserve around the treasure
- **The spring** — What the dragon always guards — water, the earth's own wealth
- **The teeth** — Violence sown into the ground, sprouting as civil strife

Greek dragons are always serpents — bearded, crested, enormous, wingless. **Ladon** on Apulian vases coils many-fold around the apple tree with Hēraklēs bargaining beside; **Python** appears on Delphic coinage beneath Apóllōn's tripod; the **Kolchian dragon** on the Naples vase hangs from the tree of the fleece with the Argonauts beneath. The constellation Draco fixed the form in the sky. Wings, legs, and fire are medieval additions: the classical drakōn is the watcher of springs and trees, and art kept him earthbound and water-tied for a thousand years.

## Epithets & Cult Titles

The Greek dragons bear epithets of place and of vigilance.

- **Πύθων (Pýthōn)** — 'the Rotter'; the Delphic serpent named from Apóllōn's taunt, "rot here."
- **Λάδων (Ládōn)** — the Hesperides' warden, named from the river of the far west he coils beside.
- **ἀκάματος** — 'unsleeping'; Apollonius' standing epithet for the Kolchian dragon — the watcher that never rests.
- **Ἰσμήνιος** — 'of the Ismēnós'; the Theban dragon's spring-title, tying him to the city's founding water.
- **δράκων** itself — 'the sharp-sighted', from δέρκομαι: the functional epithet that became the species.

## The Homeric Hymns

The Homeric Hymn to Apóllōn gives the genre's great dragonslaying: the god, seeking an oracle-site, finds the spring at Krisa guarded by "a great blooded she-dragon, a monster," who had been nurse to Typhaon and scourge of the flocks. Apóllōn's arrow kills her, and he speaks the etymology like a curse: "Now rot here (πυθεῦ) upon the fruitful soil" — whence Pythō, the Pythia, and the Pythian games. The hymn then folds the slaying into the sanctuary's charter: because she died there, the god's oracle stands there — the Greek pattern in which every holy place stands on a dragon's grave.

## Oracle Sites & Sanctuaries

The dragon's sanctuaries are the ones founded on its grave. **Delphoi** is the type-case: the temple of Apóllōn stood over Python's spring, and the Pythia prophesied above the rot the god's taunt named. At **Thebes**, the Ismenion — Apóllōn Ismēnios' temple on the hill above the Ismēnian spring — marked Kadmos' kill: Pausanias saw there the laurel and the tripod of the oracle whose founding myth is dragon-slaying. The Hesperides' garden and the Kolchian grove have no archaeology, being the map's edge, but **Kolchis'** later Phasis showed travelers the grove of the fleece as local pride.

## Archaeology & Evidence

Greek dragons are text-and-image creatures: the finest evidence is vase painting, where Python, Ladon, and the Kolchian warden appear as bearded, crested serpents from the 6th century BCE onward — a Ladon on an Apulian vase in Naples shows the many-coiled form most clearly. The dragon's civic role is epigraphic: Thebes' founding myth was official city ideology, and Athens kept a sacred snake on the Acropolis (the "guardian of the citadel" of Herodotus 8.41) as a living drakōn of the polis.

## Realm & Domain

Drákōn is not the fire-breathing hoard-guard of medieval romance but the Greeks' older idea: the enormous serpent that guards — a spring, a tree, a golden fleece, a goddess's shrine. His name comes from the verb "to see": the dragon is the one who never blinks.

### The Unsleeping Gaze

From δέρκομαι, "to see" — the dragon's defining power is vigilance, not flame.

### Python

The earth-serpent of Delphoi slain by Apóllōn, whose rotting gave the site its old name, Pythō.

### Ladon

The hundred-headed warden of the Hesperides' golden apples, coiled in the sky as Draco.

### The Sown Teeth

Kadmos killed the Ismenian dragon and planted its teeth — an armed harvest, the Spartoi, sprang up.

## Across Cultures

The Roman army adopted the draco — a hollow serpent standard with streaming windsock — from Sarmatian and Dacian cavalry, and Late Roman legions marched under dragons centuries before European heraldry claimed them. Through Latin draco the Greek watcher became the medieval dragon: hoard-guard, maiden-taker, and finally the saint-slaying beast of George and Margaret. The constellation Draco still turns around the pole, Ladon's image fixed in the sky.

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

## Cultural Legacy

Every modern "dragon" is his descendant, filtered through Latin and the Middle Ages; yet Greek dragons remained serpents — wingless, earthbound, water-tied — which is why scholars still correct the fire-lizard image. In physics and computing the name lives quietly: Draco the constellation, dragon curve fractals, and "chase the dragon" idioms all pullulate from the Greek root of the watcher who never sleeps.

## A Meditation

Drákōn guards what cannot be owned: springs, trees, thresholds. The Greeks knew that every treasure worth having is held by something that watches — and that the hero's real labour is rarely the killing but the seeing: understanding what the dragon was protecting, and why.

Every field still keeps its dragons: the unslept watcher at the edge of the mapped world, guarding the one thing the mapmaker most wants. The Greeks' honesty was to leave the watcher a reason — the spring, the tree, the fleece are never worthless — and their warning was that the slaying is never free: Kadmos founds Thebes on a dragon's grave and pays for it in generations. To name the guardian is to ask the oldest question of ambition: what does this treasure cost, and who was keeping it, and why?

## The Unicode Restoration

Drákōn is classified as **Tier 1**: the original carries both stress and length, and only one valid Unicode restoration exists. The ASCII fallback *drakon* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 6 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 2: 1 mark of stress (á); 1 mark of length (ō). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## Name Variations

The lexicon records 1 additional form of the name:

- **Drakōn** (macron-only) — LSJ convention: length only, no stress mark

The temple uses **Drákōn** as the primary form: it is the spelling that best balances philological accuracy with the practical limits of DNS.

- **k** → **k** — Same letter

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **drákōn.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode form as xn--drkn-6na36d.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Drákōn; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Greek can now be typed into any browser on earth.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does Drákōn mean?** The traditional gloss is "'The one who sees clearly' (from δέρκομαι, to see)."

**Which tradition does Drákōn belong to?** Drákōn is catalogued in the Greek pantheon of the PuniCodex lexicon.

**Why is Drákōn classified as Tier 1?** Because the original carries both stress and length, and only one valid Unicode restoration exists — and the marks in the restored spelling preserve exactly that evidence.

**Is Drákōn a working domain?** Yes — drákōn.com resolves today and routes to this temple.

**What is the punycode for drákōn.com?** The DNS encoding is xn--drkn-6na36d.com; browsers perform the translation automatically, so visitors only ever see the restored name.

**Can I use Drákōn in a normal browser?** Yes. The DNS resolves the punycode form automatically, and the type tool on this site converts drakon to Drákōn for copying and pasting.

**Where does the scholarly information come from?** The entry is built from lexica, inscriptional evidence, and reviewed scholarly sources listed in the Scholarly Edition. Every claim is traceable to a canonical source.

## Why This Restoration Matters

Every stage of the journey from Greek to Unicode was an act of care: the scribe who first wrote the name, the lexicographer who glossed it, the engineer who taught the DNS to carry it. The PuniCodex restoration is the latest stage, not the last word — the Scholarly Edition is revised as the evidence improves. What does not change is the principle: a name deserves to be written the way its own tradition wrote it. **Drákōn** in the address bar is that principle, made routable.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Drákōn**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *drakon* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 6 characters, 4 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **d** stays as it is — Same letter.

The **r** stays as it is — Same letter.

The **a** becomes **á** — Stress mark (acute/tone).

The **k** stays as it is — Same letter.

The **o** becomes **ō** — Macron marks the long vowel.

The **n** stays as it is — Same letter.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.
